basicsGuide.title: Prerequisite: Absolute Basics
basicsGuide.body: Theory Academy opens with combinatorics. If you still want to confirm hand rankings, position names, betting actions and terminology, spend a few minutes on the Strategy Academy basics wizard first — it does not count toward theory progress, but it makes every chapter after T1 easier.

drill.title: Do the Math
drill.subtitle: Apply the formula you just read. It is not scored, and you can reroll a problem and try again
drill.disclaimer: Not counted toward progress or rating
drill.incorrect: Outside the tolerance — run the formula in the hint once more

template.alpha: Pot {{pot}} bb, villain bets {{bet}} bb. What fold frequency (in %) must villain have for your bluff to break even?
template.mdf: Pot {{pot}} bb, villain bets {{bet}} bb. To stop villain bluffing with any two cards, what minimum frequency (in %) must you continue?
template.requiredEquity: Pot {{pot}} bb, villain bets {{bet}} bb. What equity (in %) do you need to call?
template.kelly: A spot wins {{winrate}}% of the time and pays {{odds}} times your risked amount when it hits. What share of your bankroll (in %) does full Kelly recommend?
template.halfKelly: Win rate {{winrate}}%, net odds {{odds}}x. What share of your bankroll (in %) does half Kelly suggest?
template.requiredHands: You win {{edge}} bb/100 with a standard deviation of {{sd}} bb/100 at z = {{z}}. Roughly how many hands separate that edge from noise?
template.riskOfRuin: Win rate {{winrate}} bb/100, std deviation {{sd}} bb/100, bankroll {{buyins}} buy-ins of 100 bb. Under the diffusion approximation, what is the risk of ruin (in %)?
template.multiwayBluffFold: Pot {{pot}} bb and you bet {{bet}} bb. If each of the {{defenders}} players still to act folds at exactly the break-even rate, what is the all-fold probability (in %)?
template.outsEquity: You have {{outs}} outs. With {{streets}} card(s) still to come, what is the exact hit probability (in %)? Use the exact formula, not the ×2/×4 rule.
template.pairCombos: Villain's range consists of {{tiers}} distinct pocket-pair ranks, and the board shows {{boardHits}} of those ranks (one card each). How many combos is the range?
template.af: A player's hand log records {{bets}} bets, {{raises}} raises and {{calls}} calls. What is his aggression factor?
template.vpip: This player voluntarily put money in the pot {{hands}} times out of {{total}} hands. What is his VPIP (in %)?

hint.mdf: MDF = P / (P + b), complementary to alpha
hint.requiredEquity: required equity = amount to call / pot after the call = b / (P + 2b)
hint.halfKelly: half Kelly = f* / 2, with f* = (b*p - q) / b
hint.requiredHands: n = (z * sigma / mu)^2; sigma = std dev (bb/100) / 10, mu = winrate (bb/100) / 100
hint.multiwayBluffFold: all-fold rate = product of the individual fold rates = alpha raised to the number of defenders
hint.pairCombos: a rank not seen on the board has 6 combos (C(4,2)); once one card of that rank is visible it has 3 (C(3,2))
hint.vpip: VPIP = voluntarily invested hands ÷ total hands × 100

prereq.title: Three things to confirm first
prereq.rule: Hand rankings and the basic rules

pl-t1-combos.question: How many combos does AKs (suited ace-king) have?
options: 4 combos
6 combos
12 combos
16 combos
pl-t1-combos.explanation: Suited combos equal the number of suits: one per suit, so 4. The 12-combo figure belongs to AKo.

pl-t1-outs.question: You have 9 outs on the flop. Roughly what is your chance of hitting by the river with two cards to come?
pl-t1-outs.explanation: Nine outs with two cards to come is about 35% (the rule of 4 gives 9 x 4 = 36; the exact value is 35.0%).

pl-t1-variance.question: Which statement about variance and the long run is correct?
options: A high win rate rules out downswings
Smaller samples reflect your true skill better
Correct decisions can still lose money for a long stretch
Variance is decided only by the opponents luck
pl-t1-variance.explanation: Correct decisions only guarantee positive expectation in the long run; short stretches can still lose, which is why bankroll and sample-size discipline matter.

pl-t2-ev.question: What does a positive expected value (EV) decision mean?
options: This particular hand will definitely win
The opponent must have made a mistake
It only holds on the river
Repeating the decision over time profits overall
pl-t2-ev.explanation: EV is a long-run average: a single trial can lose while the repeat average stays positive.

pl-t2-pot-odds.question: The pot is 100 and the opponent bets 50. Roughly what equity do you need to break even on a call?
pl-t2-pot-odds.explanation: Calling 50 makes the pot 200, so the required equity is 50 / 200 = 25%.

pl-t2-implied.question: When are implied odds most valuable?
options: You are already on the river with no bets to come
You hold an already made nut hand
Your draw can win extra chips after it hits
The pot is tiny and the opponent is short
pl-t2-implied.explanation: Implied odds price in chips you can win on later streets, so they matter most when a made draw gets paid off.

pl-t3-position.question: What is the main advantage of being in position?
options: You pay smaller blinds
You act after the opponent on every street and get more information
The rake percentage is lower
You get to see the opponents hole cards
pl-t3-position.explanation: Position is an information edge: the opponent acts first, so each of your street decisions carries more information.

pl-t3-gap.question: What is the core claim of the Gap Concept?
options: Raising needs a stronger hand than calling
Position matters more than hand strength
Any two cards are worth a limp
Calling usually needs a stronger hand than opening
pl-t3-gap.explanation: Sklansky Gap Concept: calling a raise usually demands a stronger hand than opening the betting yourself.

pl-t3-initiative.question: What does preflop initiative usually buy you after the flop?
options: You must bet every street
You may no longer check
An easier story to represent strong hands and keep barreling
The opponent is forced to fold
pl-t3-initiative.explanation: Initiative is a narrative edge: the raisers range holds more strong hands, so representing strength costs less credibility.

pl-t4-range.question: What is the key difference between range thinking and single-hand thinking?
options: Treating the opponents cards as a weighted distribution of combos
Guessing one hand and then correcting it
Only considering the opponents nuts
Only looking at your own two cards
pl-t4-range.explanation: Range thinking models the opponent as a weighted set of combos that narrows and reweights with each street of action.

pl-t4-blockers.question: What role do blockers play when choosing bluffs?
options: They make your own hand more likely to complete a straight
They raise your equity realization
They lower the rake
Holding key cards in the opponents folding range cuts their strong combos
pl-t4-blockers.explanation: Blockers are about the opponents combos: cards you hold that sit inside their strong holdings reduce how many of those they can continue with.

pl-t4-range-advantage.question: A dry ace-high flop usually favors which player?
options: The preflop caller
The preflop raiser
The big blind
Both players equally
pl-t4-range-advantage.explanation: Ace-high boards connect better with the preflop raisers range (AA, AK and AQ cluster there), so the raiser holds the range advantage.

pl-t5-mdf.question: The pot is 100 and the opponent bets 100. What is your minimum defense frequency (MDF)?

pl-t5-mixed.question: What is the point of a mixed strategy (same node, different actions by frequency)?
options: It shows you have not decided yet
It only works in casual games
It denies the opponent a stable profit from a fixed counter
Its main purpose is lowering variance
pl-t5-mixed.explanation: Mixing serves unexploitability: a fixed response becomes attackable, while frequency mixing removes the certainty a counter-strategy needs.

pl-t6-bet-purpose.question: When a hand has neither a value nor a bluff reason to bet, what is usually best?
options: Check
Bet small as a bluff
Shove for pressure
Raise the opponent
pl-t6-bet-purpose.explanation: Bets need a reason (value, bluff or protection); when none applies, checking keeps equity and controls the pot.

pl-t6-spr.question: What does a low SPR (stack-to-pot ratio) usually mean?
options: You should fine-tune sizing across many streets
The opponent will fold more often
Equity realization drops sharply
Top-pair hands can commit to all-in more comfortably
pl-t6-spr.explanation: A low SPR means one or two bets get the stacks in, which raises the commitment value of made hands like top pair.
